case_studies.title: SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: No single way of parallelizing attention serves large language models well under all loads. Low concurrency favors tensor parallelism, many independent requests favor data-parallel attention, and long prompts favor context parallelism. Reasoning, agentic, and RL-rollout workloads make a fixed choice untenable: a batch that begins as many short requests ends as a few very long ones, so the best layout changes while the same requests run. Serving engines nevertheless fix one layout at launch, because changing it has meant draining requests and restarting workers. We present SPLASH, a serving sys
case_studies.summary: SPLASH lets a LLM service switch between tensor, data, and context parallelism on the fly, solving the problem of choosing a single layout that works for all request patterns. The authors built a lightweight runtime that detects changing workloads and reconfigures the model without draining requests. This can improve utilisation and reduce latency for diverse workloads.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM serving, step 1: integrate the SPLASH runtime into your orchestration; step 2: enable workload‑aware layout switching; step 3: monitor performance and adjust thresholds for handoff.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 25/33 – The dynamic switching of parallelism layouts for LLM serving is a fresh and practical approach not previously discussed in mainstream engineering circles. IT_RELEVANCE: 20/33 – Directly impacts LLM deployment at scale, relevant for teams managing Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and cloud infra. VALUE_90_DAYS: 30/34 – Provides a clear architectural pattern and potential implementation guidelines that can be adopted within 90 days to improve performance and reduce latency. Overall score >40, so low_signal is false.

case_studies.title: EASE: Behavior-Adaptive Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents
case_studies.abstract: Agent skills provide a lightweight mechanism for self-evolving agents to accumulate reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, existing learned skill curators typically optimize curation without explicitly modeling downstream executor behavior. We show that this can cause systematic cross-executor degradation: curators trained with different executors perform best when paired with their own training executor, indicating that effective skill curation is executor-dependent. case_studies.summary: The study tackles the issue that skill curators for automated agents often perform poorly when used with different execution engines, because they don't account for the executor’s behaviour. The authors built EASE, a framework that adapts skill curation to the specific executor, and showed that this matching improves agent performance across varied executors. For a cloud infrastructure manager, the work is not directly relevant to day‑to‑day infrastructure tasks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel approach to behavior-adaptive skill curation for self-evolving agents, which introduces a new perspective on how agents can better select and reuse procedural knowledge. While the concept is technically interesting and could inform future research or internal experimentation, it does not directly translate to immediate, actionable changes in IT infrastructure, cloud or SaaS operations, or security practices that UK IT engineers typically manage. The framework’s relevance to existing MLOps or DevOps pipelines is limited, and there is no clear path to deployment or automation within a 90‑day timeframe.

case_studies.title: Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples
case_studies.abstract: Turning decoder-only large language models (LLMs) into strong dense retrievers typically requires some form of retriever training. In this paper, we ask whether LLMs can instead be prompted to produce effective representations for dense retrieval given only a few in-context examples. To answer this, we introduce RICE (Representations from In-Context Examples), a simple "training-free" approach that extracts high-quality dense representations from LLMs. To do so, RICE conditions the LLM on examples that provide a shared context for query and document encoding. Our results demonstrate that RICE
case_studies.summary: RICE shows that large language models can produce good dense retrieval vectors without any training, using only a few examples in the prompt. The authors built a simple in‑context prompting method that aligns query and document representations, and achieved retrieval performance that matches or exceeds traditional trained retrievers. This means you can skip the costly embedding model training step and still get strong search results.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a cloud search service, step 1: add a few example query‑document pairs to your prompt; step 2: let your LLM generate embeddings for new queries and documents on the fly; step 3: index those embeddings in your vector store and run nearest‑neighbour search. This flags a risk: if your org uses a custom retriever model, check whether RICE could replace it and save compute and engineering effort.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel, training‑free approach to dense retrieval using in‑context examples with LLMs. It may interest IT engineers looking to improve internal search or document retrieval systems, but the direct applicability to core infrastructure tools (SSO, cloud, endpoint management) is limited. Within 90 days a small team could prototype a search feature using RICE, but the immediate business impact is modest.

case_studies.title: Towards an AI Software Factory for Data Systems
case_studies.abstract: AI-assisted coding tools deliver significant acceleration of coding, but only limited impact across the end-to-end software development lifecycle (SDLC)--an Amdahl's law effect! In this paper, we discuss our progress towards building an AI SW Factory that accelerates all the stages of SDLC-Targeting, Coding, Reviewing, and Ops. The AI SW Factory produces a metadata exhaust that enables self-improvement by fine-tuning model weights and updating our World Model (a rich data substrate). We focus on Data Systems and the important class of Evolutionary Coding Tasks (i.e., those with a measurable ob
case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the limited reach of AI coding tools by building an AI Software Factory that speeds up every phase of the software development life‑cycle—planning, coding, review and operations—using a metadata‑driven loop to continually improve the models. The authors created a system that produces a rich metadata exhaust for data‑system projects, allowing the models to learn from each deployment. The result is faster delivery and higher quality code, with automated feedback for ongoing model refinement.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check whether your CI/CD pipelines expose deployment metadata; if so, integrate it into an automated feedback loop to fine‑tune your build tools and monitor for performance regressions. This flags a risk: if your org uses static AI‑assisted code generators without metadata tracking, you may miss opportunities to improve deployment quality.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces an AI Software Factory concept aimed at accelerating SDLC stages for data systems. While the idea shows some novelty, it remains largely academic with limited immediate applicability to the daily operations of IT engineers. The concept touches on AI-driven development and ops automation, offering moderate relevance to DevOps and MLOps practices. However, the concrete, actionable guidance or tools that could be implemented within 90 days is sparse, yielding a modest value score. Overall, the total score exceeds 40, so the paper is considered noteworthy.
